presentingComplaint: Three weeks of cough with large volumes of foul-smelling sputum, low-grade fever and weight loss.
history: Insidious onset over 3 weeks with progressive productive cough now yielding copious foul, putrid sputum, drenching night sweats, anorexia and 5 kg weight loss. Reports an episode of heavy alcohol intoxication with a witnessed vomiting/aspiration event about a month earlier. PMH: alcohol dependence, poor dentition with periodontal disease; no COPD, no immunosuppression. Ex-smoker.
examination: Cachectic, halitosis with markedly foul breath. Poor dental hygiene with gingival disease. Reduced breath sounds and bronchial breathing with coarse crepitations over the right posterior base; dullness to percussion in the same zone. No clubbing yet, no cyanosis. No neck stiffness, abdomen soft (pertinent negative: no hepatomegaly, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis).
imaging: Chest radiograph: thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level in the right lower lobe (superior segment) posterior distribution. Contrast CT chest: solitary ~5 cm cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level and surrounding consolidation, thick irregular wall, in the dependent (posterior/superior-segment) lung — typical aspiration territory.
microbiology: Sputum Gram stain shows mixed flora with foul odour suggestive of anaerobes; culture pending. Sputum AFB smear negative x1; GeneXpert MTB/RIF negative. Blood cultures pending.
differentialDiagnoses: Cavitating bronchogenic carcinoma with post-obstructive necrosis
stewardship: Empiric coverage of oral anaerobes and streptococci with IV ampicillin-sulbactam; alternative is a carbapenem or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Clindamycin is second-line due to resistance and C. difficile risk. Prolonged course (typically 3-6 weeks or until radiographic resolution). Tier: broad-spectrum beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor.
contraindications: Penicillin allergy — substitute with a respiratory fluoroquinolone plus metronidazole, or a carbapenem if non-anaphylactic
Clindamycin carries appreciable C. difficile risk; monitor for diarrhea
Avoid monotherapy that misses anaerobes (e.g., plain fluoroquinolone alone)
edgeCases: A non-resolving or right-sided cavity in a non-aspirating, non-alcoholic patient (especially a smoker over 50) mandates bronchoscopy/CT to exclude an obstructing bronchogenic carcinoma
Multiple bilateral cavities suggest septic emboli (right-sided endocarditis / Lemierre) rather than a primary aspiration abscess
Melioidosis or Klebsiella (currant-jelly) abscess in endemic/diabetic patients
expectedMaiK: Classic post-aspiration anaerobic lung abscess: solitary thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level in a dependent segment, foul sputum, indolent course with weight loss, in a patient with alcohol excess and poor dentition. Treat with prolonged anaerobe-active beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor and exclude an underlying obstructing tumour if features are atypical.
expectedNextQuestions: Was the aspiration event witnessed, and are there ongoing dysphagia or reduced-consciousness risk factors?
Any smoking history or hemoptysis raising concern for underlying malignancy?
Any TB contact, prior TB, or endemic exposure (melioidosis)?
expectedInvestigations: Contrast CT chest to characterise the cavity
Sputum culture including anaerobic and AFB/GeneXpert, plus blood cultures
Bronchoscopy if non-resolving or malignancy suspected

crossAccept.rationale: Lung abscess is a complication/continuum of aspiration pneumonia; overlapping anaerobic-cover abx.

regressionAssertions: cavitating lesion + foul sputum + aspiration risk must rank LUNG_ABSCESS above ASPIRATION_PNEUMONIA
